entry.title: 🌄 Ferienakademie 2025 – A Once-in-a-Lifetime Experience in South Tyrol 🇮🇹

link.title: 🌄 Ferienakademie 2025 – A Once-in-a-Lifetime Experience in South Tyrol 🇮🇹

entry.content:
Just returned from an incredible 2-week journey as a participant of #Ferienakademie 2025, a prestigious summer school jointly organized by Technical University of Munich (TUM), FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg, and University of Stuttgart — held in the stunning Sarntal Valley, South Tyrol, Italy.

Here’s a glimpse into this unforgettable adventure 👇

🗓️ My Experience – Week by Week Highlights

🚍 Day 1 – The Journey Begins

We started early morning as a group from all three universities, travelling together by bus to Sarntal and arriving by evening. After settling into our rooms and meeting our roommates, we had a welcome kickoff session by the professors and course coordinators.

✨ Our team won the Ice-Breaker Challenge, performing better than many previous years — a fantastic start to the program!

💼 Day 2 – Getting into the Flow

The introduction event covered Scrum, Agile methodology, and the overall project workflow. We also had a requirements session from Linova Software GmbH and Siemens Healthineers. I felt privileged to be part of the Linova team, working on a real-world challenge from industry.

🧠 Days 3–6 – Project Work Begins

We dove into project planning, architecture design, and component development. Working alongside an amazing team — Felix Kock, Isabel Zeir, Salman Salim, Alejandro, Volodymyr, Monica, and Jonas — was a rewarding experience. Despite the rainy weather in Sarentino, we kept our spirits high with short walks to enjoy nature while eagerly waiting for the hikes to start.

One of the most exciting moments was the Design Review, where we prepared a movie-style trailer for our product requirements — a creative and unique experience! 🍿

🥾 Midweek – First Hike & Cultural Immersion

We embarked on a 2–3 hour introductory hike, which was actually my first-ever hike in Germany 🏞️. Even though I’m not a hiking person, it turned out to be an unforgettable experience. The hospitality was exceptional — from delicious meals to warm interactions with everyone involved.

Unfortunately, I couldn’t join the full-day hike due to health issues for a few days, but the support and encouragement from everyone around made a huge difference.

🌆 Weekend – Exploration & Local Traditions

We spent a full day exploring Bolzano, discovering its history, culture, and charm. In the evening, we attended a traditional local event and learned about the fascinating history of the Sarentino valley.

💡 Final Days – Inspiration & Presentation

In the final stretch, we were visited by Andreas Lohr (CEO of Linova), who shared his entrepreneurial journey and inspired us with his vision and leadership.

Our final presentation was truly special — we combined role-play, GenAI, software development, system design, and even drone technology to showcase our solution. The professors were deeply impressed — in fact, they shared that our presentation was “the best they had seen in 25 years of Ferienakademie” 🎉

💭 Reflections

These two weeks were far more than just a summer school. It was about innovation, teamwork, cultural exchange, and personal growth. I learned to collaborate across disciplines, think creatively under real-world constraints, and explore new technologies while building lasting friendships.

From early morning coding sessions overlooking the Alpine peaks to evening discussions about technology and life, every moment was a learning experience. The blend of technical challenges and natural beauty created the perfect environment for creativity and collaboration.

🎤 Special thanks to Prof. Bernd Brügge, Leander Pfeiffer, Ruth, and Felix Mahr for their continuous motivation, guidance, and for creating such a transformative platform.

I return from #Ferienakademie not just with new skills — but with unforgettable memories and inspiration for the future. Already looking forward to the next one! 🚀

✍️ Written by Satya
🎓 M.Sc. Electrical Engineering, University of Stuttgart
entry.summary: A two-week adventure combining innovation, teamwork, and breathtaking Alpine landscapes – from collaborative coding to mountain hikes.

entry.title: Culture Shock on a Plate - Eating Your Way Through Stuttgart

link.title: Culture Shock on a Plate - Eating Your Way Through Stuttgart

entry.content:
🍽️ New in Stuttgart and hungry? Here’s what food habits might surprise you, what Swabians eat, and where to find dishes that taste like home.

Food is comfort, social glue, and sometimes a mini-drama. In Stuttgart, lunch starts earlier than some people even wake up, free tap water is a rare treasure, and pretzels have a legal right to be crispy. At the same time, you can taste regional legends like Spätzle and Maultaschen—or cook your own country’s food with ingredients from the many international stores. This guide shows what to expect at the table, which Swabian dishes to try, and where you can eat like a student and still feel like you’re at home.

🥨 What Surprises Many Students…

  • Lunch happens early. By 12:30 the Mensa looks like a Taylor Swift concert venue. Arrive at 11:45 and you’ll thank yourself later.
  • Splitting the bill is normal. Just say “getrennt bitte.” Voilà: German efficiency on your plate. No awkward math, no sighs.
  • Tipping is simple. Just round up a little. The first time I paid €9.20 and said “make it 10,” the waiter smiled like I’d passed a test.
  • Water is… complicated. Tap water is like a VIP guest: not always invited. Sparkling water rules. If you want still water, whisper “Leitungswasser,” cross your fingers, and prepare for side-eye.

  • Cash still matters. Cards are accepted in most spots, but your neighborhood bakery may look at your Visa like it’s Monopoly money. Keep a few coins.

  • Sunday = food survival test. Shops close. Plan ahead or you’ll end up eating pasta with ketchup. (Don’t ask how I know.)

🥟 Stuttgart Favorites (aka Swabian Soul Food)

  • Spätzle & Käsespätzle: Mac & cheese, but thicker, richer, and with so much cheese it should come with a warning. The first time I ate it, I almost needed a nap during lecture.
  • Maultaschen: Giant dumplings with meat or spinach. Monks once used them to hide meat during fasting—earning the nickname “God’s little cheat.” I call them “God’s little lifesavers during exam week.”
  • Linsen mit Spätzle: Lentils, noodles, and sausage—sounds odd, but one bite and you’ll understand why Swabians defend this dish like it’s family.
  • Zwiebelrostbraten: Beef with crispy onions. You’ll love it, your wallet won’t. My “treat yourself after a brutal exam” dish.
  • Schupfnudeln: Potato + noodles, often fried with sauerkraut. I once ordered them thinking they were pasta. Surprise! But honestly, fried potatoes in any form = happiness.

  • Schnitzel: Flat, breaded, golden-fried meat that somehow always arrives larger than the plate. The real challenge: cutting it without your fries falling on the floor.

  • Brezel: The pretzel here isn’t soft and fluffy like at baseball games. It’s got a crunchy “arm” and a soft belly. People argue which part is best—I’m team belly.

🏫 Eating on Campus: Fast, Cheap, Sometimes Surprisingly Good

Studierendenwerk Mensas and Cafés: The backbone of student survival. Cheap, filling, and there’s always at least one veggie or vegan dish.

  • Mensa Vaihingen: Feels like a food stadium. So big you might need Google Maps to find your table.
  • Cafeterias: Perfect when your lunch plan is just “coffee and a croissant count as a meal, right?”
  • The Sri Lankan & Asian food truck: Parked on campus, this food truck is the hidden gem. Officially Sri Lankan, unofficially “all of Asia in one truck.” One day it’s curry, next day it’s noodles, sometimes even fried rice that tastes like home. My friend once swore their spicy chicken revived him after an all-nighter. (Scientific proof pending.)

Pro tips:

  • Go before noon if you don’t want to queue behind half the student body.

  • Always carry your student ID—otherwise you’ll pay tourist prices.

  • Reusable boxes work, so you can sneak a second meal for dinner.

🥨 Munich Dishes You’ll Meet in Stuttgart Too

When I went to Munich, I learned two things: one, Bavarians love food you can’t pronounce; two, breakfast can include beer.

  • Weißwurst: White sausages eaten before noon. Locals say after twelve the sausages “die.” I ate one at two p.m. and lived, but don’t tell anyone.
  • Obatzda: Cheese spread with paprika. Looks like pumpkin baby food, tastes like heaven with pretzels.

  • Leberkäse: No liver. No cheese. Just a mysterious meat block in bread. I don’t ask questions anymore—I just eat it.

  • Hendl: Roast chicken. At Oktoberfest, I saw someone demolish an entire chicken in under 10 minutes. Inspiring.

🎄 Christmas Market (aka Calorie Wonderland)

I swore I’d “just look” at the Weihnachtsmarkt. Ten minutes later, I had candied almonds, a bratwurst, and Nutella crêpes in both hands. Self-control? Never heard of her.

  • Glühwein: Hot spiced wine that tastes like Christmas and sneaks up on you after the second mug.
  • Kinderpunsch: Non-alcoholic version. Safe for kids… or for you when you have a morning lecture next day.
  • Gebrannte Mandeln: Sugar-roasted almonds. You’ll smell them first, follow your nose, and suddenly your wallet is lighter.

  • Flammkuchen: Thin crispy bread with cream, onions, and bacon. Germany’s idea of pizza—but lighter and crispier.

  • Crêpes with Nutella: Technically French, but at German Christmas markets they’ve been adopted like international exchange students.

🍲 Eating Like at Home (and Sometimes Better)

  • Cook with friends: The cheapest, funniest, and most international dinner party you’ll ever host. Everyone brings one dish from their country—boom, instant world buffet in your WG kitchen. Pro tip: label allergens so your Italian friend doesn’t cry after accidentally eating chili.
  • German BBQ: Here, a tiny disposable grill plus a pack of sausages = official German summer. Bring potato salad, some buns, and you’ve unlocked level 100 “local student.”

  • Temples = mini India: Feeling homesick? Stuttgart has both a Gurudwara and the Vinayaka temple. You’ll find community vibes, delicious langar or prasad, and sometimes even that comforting smell of chai that instantly feels like home.

  • YouTube chef mode: Don’t know how to cook? No excuses. YouTube is basically a free culinary school. I went from “burns water” to “semi-decent curry chef” in one semester. Try it—it’s cheaper than Lieferando.

🍛 Restaurants Worth Exploring

  • Indian: Biryani so good you’ll forget you’re in Germany.
  • Vietnamese: Fresh summer rolls and that magical pho broth.
  • Thai: Mango chicken rice = happiness on a plate.
  • Indonesian: Fried rice with a spicy kick.
  • Turkish: Baklava sweeter than your crush’s texts.
  • Döner shops: The unofficial student fuel of Stuttgart.

  • Chinese: Hakka noodles, wok-fried and wallet-friendly.

  • Milaneo Mall & Stadtmitte: Food paradise under one roof. From McDonald’s and KFC (yes, sometimes you just need fries at midnight) to sushi, burgers, ramen, or bubble tea—it’s all here. Basically, Milaneo is where diets go to die, but in the happiest way.

🛒 Shopping Tips (a.k.a. Where Students Actually Live)

  • Aldi Süd & Kaufland: These two are basically student HQs. Need cheap pasta, frozen pizza, or snacks for an all-nighter? Aldi is your hero. Want a supermarket where you can find everything from bread to Bluetooth speakers? Kaufland is your next home. Seriously, half of student life happens between its aisles.
  • Rewe: The “posh cousin” of Aldi. Prices are a bit higher, but the food looks fresher, the stores smell nicer, and—bonus—you can shop late (some are open till midnight). Perfect for that 11 p.m. “oops I forgot milk” moment.
  • Indian store (Stuttgart): The lifeline for curry cravings and spice emergencies. Recently, they even opened a small food stall—so now you can grab fresh samosas, papdi chaat, or a steaming cup of masala chai while shopping. I went “just for cumin seeds” and left with a plate of chaat and a happy stomach.
  • Khan Market: No, not Delhi—this one in Stuttgart! Packed with South Asian spices, lentils, and pickles. It’s the place where you suddenly realize you can cook like at home.
  • TEDi: The fun, cheap store for decorations, stationery, and random stuff you didn’t know you needed. Enter for a pen, leave with fairy lights, a giant mug, and Halloween napkins. Don’t ask.

  • Action: Not as famous among students, but definitely worth it. Think of it as TEDi’s cousin—household goods, cleaning stuff, decorations. Sometimes it even beats IKEA for small finds.

  • IKEA: Yes, furniture exists. But let’s be real: most students go for hot dogs and soft-serve ice cream, not the shelves. I once left with zero furniture but three hot dogs. Priorities.

🍴 Final Bite

Here’s the truth: you’ll survive on pasta and toast for a while, then discover Spätzle, dumplings, and Christmas crêpes, and suddenly Stuttgart feels like home. My advice? Embrace the quirks, laugh at the culture shocks, and never—never—forget to buy groceries on Saturday!

Welcome to Germany! You made it!

✍️ Written by Satya 🎓 M.Sc. Electrical Engineering, University of Stuttgart
entry.summary: New in Stuttgart? Discover the food habits, Swabian dishes, and student survival tips that will surprise you—and help you feel at home.

entry.title: Deutschland Stipdendium (The German National Scholarship)
entry.content:
That's me receiving my scholarship certificate from the committee.

🎓 A Scholarship That Opens Doors …

Discover how the Deutschlandstipendium shaped my academic journey in Germany—from cultural integration to professional growth.

The Deutschlandstipendium isn’t just financial support—it’s a powerful gateway to academic excellence, intercultural exchange, and professional opportunities. As an international student, I found not only funding but a sense of belonging, purpose, and connection to German society.

🚀 A Journey of Growth, Belonging & Pride…

When I landed in Germany as an international student, I carried hopes, questions, and ambition. What I didn’t expect was how a single scholarship—the Deutschlandstipendium (DStip)—would open doors I hadn’t even imagined. This isn’t just a scholarship. It’s a catalyst. A bridge between dreams and reality. Between students and industry. Between cultures and connections.

✍️ Applying for the Deutschlandstipendium…

Every year, the University of Stuttgart opens its DStip application window around mid-January (usually the 16th–25th), with funding starting in April. You’ll receive an initial email in late December or early January announcing the timeline.

The scholarship is open to all students enrolled at the University of Stuttgart, regardless of their current semester, as long as they’re within the standard study period (≤4 semesters for Master’s, ≤6 for Bachelor’s). Yes—even first-semester international students can apply!

📌 I was fortunate to receive this prestigious scholarship twice:

  • April 2023 – March 2024
  • April – September 2024 (during my final semester in M.Sc. Electrical Engineering)

💡 What DStip Represents…

This isn’t just a scholarship—it’s a recognition of academic excellence, social engagement, and personal motivation. With only about 157–159 recipients selected annually, being chosen feels like a true honor.

As a student from India, the DStip opened the door to meaningful cultural immersion in Germany. It enabled me to contribute to a diverse academic community while integrating into society on both personal and professional levels.

🧠 Tips to Maximize Your Chances…

  • Strong Grades: Aim for 1.0–2.0 (especially from your Bachelor’s, if you’re applying early in your Master’s).
  • Work Experience: Internships, seminars, and workshops make your profile shine.
  • Volunteer & Extracurricular Work: This matters more than you think!
  • Motivation Letter: Be humble, honest, and show purpose.
  • Document Every Claim: Use consistent labels and attachments.
  • Start Early: Last-minute applications feel rushed—and committees can tell.

💬 Remember: You don’t need to be perfect—just authentic, driven, and prepared.

🔍 How They Evaluate…

Selection is based on a balanced profile:

  • Academic performance
  • Community involvement
  • Motivation
  • Potential for future contributions

Applications are ranked faculty-wise using a structured point system, and final selections are made after manual verification.

🤝 The Sponsors: More Than Just Donors…

Each DStip is co-funded:

  • 50% by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF)
  • 50% by private sponsors like companies, individuals, or foundations. For me, they were Vishay Semiconductors GmbH and Christian Bürkert Stiftung, one for each year.

You can indicate up to 3 sponsor preferences, though final pairing is based on availability.

My Experience…

Over the two years, I had two different sponsors. I reached out, visited their offices, joined their events, and even got invited to Engineers’ Day celebrations. From friendly emails to Christmas gifts, these companies made me feel seen and valued.

🌟 The May/June Ceremony – A Moment of Pride…

One of the most heartwarming highlights of receiving the Deutschlandstipendium is the official award ceremony, typically held in May or June.

It’s not just a formal event—it’s a celebration:

  • You’re awarded a certificate of achievement
  • You meet and greet with eminent industry leaders, sponsors, professors, and fellow scholars
  • You’re encouraged to bring a guest for free—a friend, a mentor, or family member to share your joy
  • There’s food, laughter, networking, and tons of proud moments

🎉 This evening remains one of the most fulfilling experiences in my academic life—an event where hard work truly feels honored.

💶 Beyond the €300/month – What It Really Gave Me…

Sure, the money helps. But that’s just the beginning.

  • I used the support to travel, attend research conferences, and go on hikes and get-togethers with German friends.
  • I explored personal development, built a portfolio, and self-funded small side-projects.
  • I gained confidence, lowered stress, and made my family proud.
  • Most importantly, I felt recognized—and that feeling is priceless.

📢 My Message to Future Applicants…

If you’re even thinking about it—go for it. Apply.

This scholarship isn’t about being the best. It’s about showing the real you: someone committed, curious, and ready to grow.

💬 One important note: You can’t receive two public scholarships at the same time. So plan wisely.

🔁 Reapplication is possible next year—you can apply either from scratch or reuse previous documents if stated. Just keep your grades strong and stay engaged.

🌍 More Than a Scholarship—A Community…

The Deutschlandstipendium fosters a multicultural, merit-based, and forward-looking academic culture. It brings together students, companies, and institutions under a shared vision: to build a better future—together.

So whether you’re at the start of your journey or deep into your studies, believe in this:

✨ One well-written application can change everything.
Doors will open. People will notice. And you’ll realize—you belong.

❤️ Trust the Process. Trust Yourself…

It’s not just the destination that shapes us. It’s every form you fill, every word you write, every challenge you face. It’s the journey that makes the victory meaningful.

So, to whoever’s reading this:
You’ve got this.
Believe in your story. Write it well.

📸 Bonus: I’ll soon share moments from the award ceremony and networking events on my blog—stay tuned!

✍️ Written by Satya
🎓 M.Sc. Electrical Engineering, University of Stuttgart
🏅 Deutschlandstipendium Awardee (2023–2024 & 2024)
entry.summary: The scholarship that changed my life.
